lessons.t: Why speed and accuracy pull against each other
lessons.intro: You will learn why rushing and checking too long both cost points on timed tests. Knowing the trade-off lets you choose your pace on purpose.

cards.b: Each answer costs time and carries a chance of error. Spend too little time and mistakes rise, spend too much and you run out of questions.
Accuracy usually stays high at a comfortable pace, then drops sharply once you push past it. The point where errors start climbing is the one to find.
The best total score comes from the pace just before accuracy falls off. Treat that pace as your target rather than your absolute fastest speed.

fig.title: Error rate (%) at three paces
fig.note: Errors rise sharply once you rush past your steady pace.

ex.q: Pace A answers 30 questions in 30 minutes with 90% correct. Pace B answers 40 questions in 40 minutes with 60% correct. Which gives more correct answers in total?
ex.why: Pace A gives 30 x 0.9 = 27 correct answers. Pace B gives 40 x 0.6 = 24 correct answers, so the careful pace scores higher.

lessons.tip: Measure your accuracy at each pace before you decide what speed to aim for.

quiz.q: Which pace usually gives the best total score?
o: The pace just before accuracy drops
The slowest pace you can manage
quiz.why: Accuracy holds up until a point, so the best total sits just below the point where errors climb.

quiz.q: If accuracy drops sharply when you speed up, what does that show?
o: You have passed your best pace
quiz.why: A sharp drop means you have moved past the pace where accuracy stays high.

lessons.t: Finding your personal working pace
lessons.intro: You will learn a simple way to test your own speed and accuracy. Knowing your pace lets you plan each section of a test with confidence.

cards.b: Take a 10 minute practice set and time yourself on every question. Record how many you attempt and how many you get right.
Divide questions attempted by minutes to get questions per minute. If you attempted 20 questions in 10 minutes, your rate is 2 per minute.
Repeat the set one notch faster and check whether accuracy holds above about 85 percent. Keep the fastest pace where it still does.

fig.title: Finding your pace
fig.note: Repeat weekly as your skill grows.

ex.q: You attempt 24 questions in 12 minutes and get 20 right. What is your accuracy, and what is your rate per minute?
ex.why: Accuracy is 20 divided by 24, about 83 percent. Rate is 24 attempts divided by 12 minutes, which is 2 per minute.

lessons.tip: Judge your pace by accuracy first and speed second.

quiz.q: You attempt 30 questions in 15 minutes. What is your rate per minute?
quiz.why: Divide 30 attempts by 15 minutes to get 2 per minute.

quiz.q: Your accuracy falls to 60 percent at a faster pace. What should you do?
quiz.why: Dropping below your accuracy threshold means the faster pace costs more than it gains.

lessons.t: Reading the question before answering
lessons.intro: You will learn how one missed word, such as not or except, can turn a correct method into a wrong answer. Careful reading protects your speed over the whole test.

cards.b: Words like not, except, least and always flip what the question asks for. Spot them before you look at the options.
Put the question in your own short words before scanning the choices. This stops you matching an option that answers a different question.
Once you pick an option, reread the question stem for one second. A quick check catches flipped logic before it costs a point.

fig.title: Careful versus hasty reading
fig.note: Both pick quickly, only one checks the stem.

ex.q: Which of these is NOT an even number?
ex.why: 25 is odd because it leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 2. The other three all divide by 2 exactly.

lessons.tip: Read the question word by word, then look at the answers.

quiz.q: Which option is NOT a prime number: 7, 9, 11 or 13?
quiz.why: 9 is 3 times 3, so it is not prime, while 7, 11 and 13 are prime.

quiz.q: What should you do before choosing an option?
o: Restate the question in your own words
Pick the one you saw first
quiz.why: A short restatement stops you matching an option that answers a different question.

lessons.t: Estimate first to catch big errors
lessons.intro: You will learn to round numbers and estimate an answer before calculating. A rough estimate catches the large slips that cost the most points.

cards.b: Change 48 to 50 and 19 to 20 when you need a quick answer. Rounding keeps the mental arithmetic fast and easy to follow.
Work out a rough answer and see which option sits closest. If your exact result is far from the estimate, recheck the steps.
Estimate first, then calculate exactly only when two options are close. Save the full working for those close calls.

fig.title: 48 x 19 exact and rounded
fig.note: Rounding gives a close estimate, within about 10 percent.

ex.q: What is a quick estimate for 39 times 11, found by rounding 39 to 40 and 11 to 10?
ex.why: Round 39 up to 40 and 11 down to 10, giving 40 times 10 = 400. The exact answer is 429, so 400 is a close and quick check.

lessons.tip: Estimate first, then check your exact answer against it.

quiz.q: Round 62 and 29 to 60 and 30. What is the estimate for 62 times 29?
quiz.why: 60 times 30 is 1800, and the exact answer is 1798.

quiz.q: Why estimate before calculating?
o: It removes the need to calculate
quiz.why: A rough answer shows whether a precise result is far off, so you can recheck it.

lessons.t: Spotting careless error patterns
lessons.intro: You will learn to recognise the slips you make most often under time pressure. Naming your own pattern lets you guard against it on the next test.

cards.b: Review your last practice set and sort each wrong answer by type. Most people repeat the same two or three kinds of slip.
Typical slips include misreading a sign, copying a digit wrongly and skipping a step in a sequence. These happen fastest when your attention drifts.
Pick one check for your top slip, such as rereading signs before you answer. One targeted check costs seconds and removes a repeat mistake.

fig.title: Slips in one practice set
fig.note: Fix the largest bar first, since it wins the most points.

ex.q: In a practice set you made 6 sign errors, 4 digit errors, 3 skipped steps and 1 other slip. Which slip should you target first?
ex.why: Sign errors are the largest group at 6 of the 14 slips, so fixing them recovers the most marks.

lessons.tip: Name your most common slip so you can catch it on purpose.

quiz.q: What is the best first step to find your own error pattern?
o: Sort your wrong answers by type
quiz.why: Sorting wrong answers by type shows which slip repeats most often.

quiz.q: Which check suits a habit of misreading signs?
quiz.why: Rereading the sign costs a few seconds and directly targets the slip.

lessons.t: Building accuracy with short focused drills
lessons.intro: You will learn how five minute drills build both speed and accuracy. Short sessions keep your attention sharp and make practice easy to repeat.

cards.b: A five minute drill keeps effort high and errors easy to review. Longer sessions tend to fade, so stop while you still feel focused.
Practise one question type until it feels automatic. Familiar layouts free attention for the reasoning that actually earns marks.
Write down how many you got right in each drill. Improvement shows up as a rising score at the same pace.

fig.title: The drill loop
fig.note: Repeat daily for steady gains.

ex.q: You score 8 out of 10 in one five minute drill and 9 out of 10 in the next. Which change matters most?
ex.why: Your score went from 80 percent to 90 percent over the same length of drill, so accuracy rose by 10 percentage points.

lessons.tip: Stop a drill while you still feel sharp, not when you are exhausted.

quiz.q: A drill has 10 questions and you get 7 right. What is your accuracy?
quiz.why: 7 correct out of 10 is 70 percent.

quiz.q: Why repeat the same question format in drills?
o: It removes the need to think
quiz.why: Familiar layouts become automatic, so more attention goes to the reasoning itself.

lessons.t: Pacing yourself across a whole test
lessons.intro: You will learn how to split a timed test into a time budget per question. A simple budget keeps you from running out of time on the last page.

cards.b: Divide the total minutes by the number of questions to get a base budget. A 60 minute test with 40 questions gives 1.5 minutes each.
Answer the quick questions first and keep a note of the time you saved. That buffer pays for a harder question later.
Look at the time every ten questions and compare it with your budget. If you are behind, speed up only on the easy items.

fig.title: Minutes left at checkpoints
fig.note: Each quarter of a 60 minute test uses 15 minutes.

ex.q: A test has 60 minutes and 40 questions. After 20 questions you have 25 minutes left. Are you on track?
o: Behind, you should have 30 minutes left
ex.why: After 20 questions you should have used 30 minutes, leaving 30. Having 25 left means you are about 5 minutes behind.

lessons.tip: Watch the clock at set points, not after every single question.

quiz.q: A 90 minute test has 30 questions. What is the base time per question?
quiz.why: 90 divided by 30 is 3 minutes per question.

quiz.q: When should you speed up?
o: Only on the easy questions when behind
On every question at all times
quiz.why: Speeding up on easy items recovers time without rushing the hardest questions.

lessons.t: Moving on from a question that stalls you
lessons.intro: You will learn when to leave a hard question and come back later. Stalling on one item can cost you several easy marks at the end.

cards.b: Decide in advance how long any single question may take, such as twice your base budget. When you reach the cap, mark it and move on.
Choose your best provisional answer, flag the question, and keep moving. Returning later with fresh eyes often clears the problem quickly.
Each stalled minute is a minute taken from easier questions you could answer. Treat the flag as a fair use of your time, not as giving up.

fig.title: Handling a stalled question
fig.note: Return only if time remains at the end.

ex.q: Your base budget is 90 seconds per question and your cap is twice that. After 3 minutes on one question, what should you do?
ex.why: The cap is twice 90 seconds, which is 3 minutes. Once you reach it, flag the question and move to the next one.

lessons.tip: A flagged question you return to is worth more than a stuck one.

quiz.q: What does a time cap help you avoid?
o: Spending too long on one item
quiz.why: A cap stops one difficult question from taking time away from many easier ones.

quiz.q: On returning to a flagged question, what is the best move?
o: Reconsider it with fresh eyes if time allows
Leave it blank no matter what
quiz.why: Fresh eyes often spot the flaw, and a provisional answer means you never leave it blank.

lessons.t: Taking short breaks to protect focus
lessons.intro: You will learn how brief breaks restore attention during long practice sessions. Planned rest keeps your accuracy steady from the first minute to the last.

cards.b: Concentration tends to drop after about 25 to 30 minutes of intense work. Errors creep in quietly before you notice them.
Work for 25 minutes, then rest for 5 minutes, and repeat the cycle. The clear boundary makes it easier to return to the task.
Stand up, look at something far away, or drink some water. Avoid scrolling a screen, which keeps your mind busy and tired.

fig.title: Accuracy (%) across one session
fig.note: Typical pattern: accuracy dips before a break and recovers after.

ex.q: Study uses 25 minutes of work and 5 minutes of rest. How many full cycles fit into a 60 minute session?
ex.why: One cycle is 25 plus 5, which is 30 minutes. Two cycles fill the 60 minutes exactly.

lessons.tip: Take the break before you feel tired, not after.

quiz.q: What is one typical work length before a short break?
quiz.why: Concentration tends to fade after roughly half an hour of intense work.

quiz.q: Which break activity best restores focus?
quiz.why: Looking into the distance rests the eyes and mind, while screens keep attention busy.

lessons.t: Learning from every error you make
lessons.intro: You will learn a simple review method that turns each mistake into a faster, more accurate habit. A short review after each set beats hours of unfocused practice.

cards.b: Start with each question you got wrong and work out why. Note whether the cause was knowledge, speed, or a careless slip.
Solve the same question again without looking at the answer. If you can do it cleanly, the lesson has stuck.
Turn each mistake into a short rule, such as always check the units. Read your rules before the next session to keep them fresh.

fig.title: The error review routine
fig.note: Run this after every practice set.

ex.q: You got 4 questions wrong in a 20 question set. What is your accuracy, and what should you review first?
ex.why: You got 16 right out of 20, which is 80 percent. Reviewing the 4 wrong answers first targets the gaps quickly.

lessons.tip: A mistake reviewed properly is worth more than a correct answer guessed.

quiz.q: What is the best reason for redoing a question you got wrong?
o: To avoid reading the question again
To check the fix really works
quiz.why: Solving it again without the answer shows whether you can now reach the right answer yourself.

quiz.q: What makes a good written rule?
quiz.why: A short, specific rule is easy to read before a session and easy to apply under pressure.

lessons.t: Scanning a grid to find a target letter
lessons.intro: You will learn a systematic way to scan a grid of letters for one target. A steady sweep finds the match faster than looking at random.

cards.b: Move your eyes left to right across each row, then drop to the next row. A fixed route stops you missing cells or checking the same ones twice.
Hold the target in mind before you start, and scan for its exact letters. Filtering on one feature speeds up the search a lot.
Use your finger or a pen on paper to keep your place. Losing your place is the biggest cause of slow, repeated scanning.

fig.title: Find the first Q
fig.note: Scan left to right, then drop a row.

ex.q: Scan this grid row by row. Row 1: A B C. Row 2: D Z E. Row 3: Z F G. Where is the first Z?
ex.why: Row 1 has no Z, so the scan moves to row 2, where Z sits in the middle column. That is the first Z you reach.

lessons.tip: Keep one eye on the target and one on the route.

quiz.q: Why use a fixed scanning route?
o: It is quicker to read numbers
quiz.why: A fixed route covers every cell once, so nothing is skipped or repeated.

quiz.q: What is the most common cause of slow scanning?
o: Losing your place in the grid
quiz.why: Losing your place forces you to rescan rows, which wastes time.

lessons.t: Sweeping systematically through a list
lessons.intro: You will learn to sweep a long list of items in order, without skipping. A consistent method beats rushing back and forth across the page.

cards.b: Pick top to bottom and left to right, then use it every time. Switching orders mid-search creates gaps and duplicate checks.
Set a pace you can hold for the whole list. A rhythm keeps your eyes moving rather than stopping to think at each item.
When you find a match, check it fully before you record it. Quick confirmation prevents false hits in dense lists.

fig.title: Reading order of a list
fig.note: Read down column A first, then move to column B.

ex.q: You must scan a table of 20 cells and you check 3 cells per second. About how many seconds does the full scan take?
ex.why: There are 20 cells, and at 3 cells per second the scan takes 20 divided by 3, about 7 seconds.

lessons.tip: A consistent order is faster than a clever one you cannot repeat.

quiz.q: What goes wrong when you switch reading order mid-search?
quiz.why: Switching order makes it easy to skip cells or check the same one twice.

quiz.q: Why confirm a match before recording it?
o: To prevent false hits in dense lists
quiz.why: A quick confirmation catches look-alike items that only seem to match at a glance.

lessons.t: Finding one letter inside a block of text
lessons.intro: You will learn to hunt for a single letter or word in dense text. Scanning for word shapes and first letters keeps the search quick and reliable.

cards.b: Look at the length and first letter of each word rather than reading every one. Matching the shape narrows the search very quickly.
Read the text in groups of three or four words at a time. Chunks keep your eyes moving and make it easier to notice a missing or extra letter.
Note the position of your first match if the task asks for it. Then continue from that point rather than starting again.

fig.title: Chunked text scan
fig.note: Repeat chunk by chunk until the end.

ex.q: How many times does the letter s appear in the word 'lesson'?
ex.why: The word lesson has two letter s, one after the e and one after the other s. Counting letter by letter gives 2.

lessons.tip: Scan word shapes first, then check letters only where shapes match.

quiz.q: What is a quick way to narrow a text search?
o: Match the length and first letter
Look only at the last line
quiz.why: Matching shape and first letter removes most words without reading each one fully.

quiz.q: Why read text in chunks of three or four words?
o: It keeps your eyes moving and helps you spot letters
quiz.why: Chunks keep the eyes moving steadily, which makes missing or extra letters easier to notice.

lessons.t: Spotting the odd one out quickly
lessons.intro: You will learn to find the item that differs from a set without checking every detail. Focusing on the one feature that changes saves a lot of time.

cards.b: Pick the one attribute most likely to vary, such as colour, size or direction. Checking one feature at a time is quicker than comparing everything at once.
Compare each item with its neighbour, then move along the set. Pairs make differences stand out quickly.
When one item clearly breaks the pattern, select it without re-checking the rest. Verify only when two items look close.

fig.title: Two ways to find the odd one

pts: Stop at the first clear odd

fig.note: Feature scans are quicker for most sets.

ex.q: Which is the odd one out in 4, 8, 12, 15, 16?
ex.why: Every other number in the list is even, and 15 is the only odd one, so it is the odd one out.

lessons.tip: Check the feature that is most likely to change first.

quiz.q: Which feature is the best first one to check when comparing shapes?
o: The one most likely to vary
quiz.why: Checking the most variable feature finds the difference fastest.

quiz.q: When should you recheck the items before selecting?
o: When two items look very close
When one item clearly breaks the pattern
Only at the end of the test
quiz.why: Close calls need a second look, while a clear break in the pattern can be chosen straight away.

lessons.t: Scanning a long list of numbers
lessons.intro: You will learn to find a target number in a long run of figures. Grouping the numbers into chunks makes the scan faster and less error-prone.

cards.b: Read long numbers in groups of three digits, as you would see with commas. Chunks make it easier to match a target without losing your place.
In an ordered list, notice where the numbers stop climbing or start repeating. A break in the pattern often marks the item you need.
If the numbers are sorted, skip ahead by halves rather than checking each one. This halving approach finds a value in far fewer steps.

fig.title: A sorted list to search
fig.note: Halve the range each check to find 31 quickly.

ex.q: You are searching the sorted list 3, 7, 12, 19, 25, 31, 40, 48 for 31. Your first check is at 19, which is too low. Which part should you search next?
ex.why: Because 19 is less than 31, every value below 19 is also too small, so the search continues in the upper half above 19.

lessons.tip: On a sorted list, use the order to skip large chunks.

quiz.q: Why group long numbers in threes?
o: It keeps your place while matching
quiz.why: Chunks help you track where you are, so a target is matched without rescanning.

quiz.q: On a sorted list, what does a halving search give you?
o: Far fewer checks than scanning each item
quiz.why: Halving discards half the remaining items on every check, so it needs far fewer steps.

lessons.t: Keeping your gaze steady while scanning
lessons.intro: You will learn how to use wider vision to take in more of a page at once. A steady gaze reduces the back and forth movement that slows you down.

cards.b: Rest your gaze at the middle of a block and take in the items around it. Moving your eyes less often cuts the time lost to refocusing.
Let your attention spread across a whole row rather than one item at a time. With practice you can read several items per glance.
Tension narrows attention and makes you blink and tense up. Take one slow breath and soften your shoulders before each new block.

fig.title: Steady scanning rhythm
fig.note: Let the rows come to you rather than chasing each item.

ex.q: A page has 60 items in 6 rows of 10. If you take in 2 full rows per glance, how many glances does the page need?
ex.why: Each glance covers 2 rows, and 6 rows divided by 2 gives 3 glances.

lessons.tip: Let the rows come to you rather than chasing each item.

quiz.q: What does a steady gaze reduce?
quiz.why: Fewer refocusing moves means each glance covers more items, which saves time.

quiz.q: Why relax your shoulders before scanning a block?
quiz.why: Tension narrows attention and slows your eyes, so relaxing widens the field you can take in.

lessons.t: Locating a value in a two-way table
lessons.intro: You will learn to find a value by reading a row and a column together. This skill appears often in data questions and must be fast.

cards.b: Locate the row heading that matches your target, and run your eye across it. Working from the label keeps you in the right part of the table.
Drop down from the column heading to meet your row. The cell where the two lines cross holds the value you need.
Confirm both headings before you read the number. Many errors come from using a neighbouring row or column.

fig.title: Sales by shop and month
fig.note: Find Shop A, then move across to Feb.

ex.q: Shop A sold 12 in Jan and 15 in Feb. Shop B sold 8 in Jan and 14 in Feb. What did Shop B sell in February?
ex.why: Find the Shop B row, then move across to the February column. The cell where they meet holds 14.

lessons.tip: Read the row label and the column label before you read the number.

quiz.q: What should you locate first in a two-way table?
quiz.why: The row heading tells you which row to read, and the column heading then narrows it to one cell.

quiz.q: Shop A sold 12 in January, 15 in February and 9 in March. What was March's value?
quiz.why: March is the third value in the Shop A row, which is 9.

lessons.t: Hunting for repeats inside a set
lessons.intro: You will learn how to spot duplicate items quickly in a list or set of codes. Systematic checking avoids both missed repeats and false alarms.

cards.b: Arrange the items in order, such as alphabetical or numerical, so twins sit next to each other. Sorted sets make duplicates much easier to see.
Check every item against the one directly after it. This single comparison catches most repeats in an ordered list.
Write down duplicates as you find them so you do not recount. Keeping a tally makes the final answer reliable.

fig.title: Items found in a list
fig.note: Repeats are the total minus the unique items.

ex.q: A list has 12 codes. After removing duplicates, 9 unique codes remain. How many repeats were there?
ex.why: 12 codes minus 9 unique codes leaves 3 repeated entries.

lessons.tip: Sort first, then compare neighbours, and the twins reveal themselves.

quiz.q: Why sort a list before checking for repeats?
o: Matching items end up next to each other
It is not useful at all
quiz.why: Once sorted, identical items sit together, so neighbour checks catch them.

quiz.q: What is the best way to avoid recounting a repeat?
o: Write each repeat down as you find it
quiz.why: A written tally keeps the count accurate without needing to rescan.

lessons.t: Scanning with a mental template
lessons.intro: You will learn to hold a template of the target in mind so you can recognise it instantly. A clear template turns a slow hunt into a quick match.

cards.b: Before scanning, state what you are looking for in one short phrase. A precise template is easier to match than a vague idea.
Let the template act like a filter, passing over anything that clearly fails. Only slow down for items that come close to matching.
If the task rule changes, update your template before you start again. Scanning for the old target wastes whole passes.

fig.title: Template scanning routine
fig.note: Repeat for each new item in the set.

ex.q: Your template is 'a multiple of 5 and greater than 40'. Which of 35, 45, 50 and 62 match?
ex.why: 35 is below 40 and 62 is not a multiple of 5. So 45 and 50 match both parts of the template.

lessons.tip: Phrase the target in one line so you can match it at a glance.

quiz.q: What makes a good scanning template?
o: A vague feeling about the target
A list of every possible answer
quiz.why: A precise one line description is quick to hold and easy to match against each item.

quiz.q: When should you update your template?
o: Only when the task rule changes
At the end of the test
quiz.why: Scanning for an outdated target wastes passes, so update it whenever the rule changes.

lessons.t: Dividing a big field into zones
lessons.intro: You will learn to split a large field of items into zones before you scan. Zoning turns an overwhelming search into a series of small, manageable sweeps.

cards.b: Mentally divide a large grid into four equal zones, such as top left and bottom right. Each zone is small enough to scan in one pass.
Finish the top left zone completely before moving on to the next. Jumping between zones makes you lose track of what you have checked.
Record how many matches each zone holds as you finish it. Zone totals help you check the final answer against your running notes.

fig.title: Four zones of a grid
fig.note: Scan each quarter fully before moving on.

ex.q: A 4 by 4 grid is split into four zones of 2 by 2. If you scan one zone in 6 seconds, how long do all four zones take?
ex.why: There are four zones at 6 seconds each, which is 4 times 6, or 24 seconds in total.

lessons.tip: Finish each zone before starting the next, and your count stays honest.

quiz.q: How many zones does a 4 by 4 grid split into when using 2 by 2 zones?
quiz.why: A 4 by 4 grid holds four 2 by 2 blocks, so there are four zones.

quiz.q: Why keep a running count for each zone?
o: It lets you check the final answer
It removes the need to confirm matches
quiz.why: Zone totals give you a record to check your final number against.

lessons.t: Committing to an answer with confidence
lessons.intro: You will learn how to commit to an answer once the evidence is good enough. Decisive choices protect your time and reduce second guessing.

cards.b: Decide the level of evidence you need before you choose, such as eliminating two options. Clear criteria stop you reopening settled questions.
When the evidence reaches your standard, select the option and move on. Continuing to reconsider rarely improves the score.
Feeling unsure is normal, especially on hard items. Accept the uncertainty and keep your pace, since doubt alone is not new evidence.

fig.title: Seconds per item by style
fig.note: Seconds per item, a common pattern for these two styles.

ex.q: Your rule is to commit once you have eliminated two of four options. You have just eliminated two. What should you do?
o: Choose one of the remaining options
ex.why: Your criterion is met, so you commit to one of the two options that remain instead of reopening the question.

lessons.tip: Decide your standard before the question starts, not during it.

quiz.q: Why set a standard for a decision in advance?
o: It stops the review of every question
It stops you reopening settled questions
quiz.why: A standard in advance gives you a clear point to stop, so you can move on.

quiz.q: Feeling a little doubt after choosing means what?
o: Doubt alone is not new evidence
quiz.why: Doubt is a feeling, not information, so it should not reverse a well-reasoned choice.

lessons.t: Setting a confidence threshold for answers
lessons.intro: You will learn to set a confidence level that tells you when an answer is good enough. A threshold keeps your decisions quick and consistent.

cards.b: Give each provisional answer a score from one, a wild guess, to five, certain. A simple scale turns a vague feeling into a usable number.
Choose a minimum score, such as three, below which you flag and move on. Setting it beforehand removes the need to decide on the spot.
Compare your confidence scores with how often you were right in practice. If your fours are right only half the time, be more cautious and raise your threshold.

fig.title: Commit or flag rules
fig.note: A simple rule keeps decisions quick.

ex.q: Your threshold is 3 out of 5. You score a question 2. What should you do?
ex.why: A score of 2 is below your threshold of 3, so you flag the question and keep your pace.

lessons.tip: Write your threshold at the top of your practice notes.

quiz.q: On a one to five scale, what does a score of 1 suggest?
quiz.why: A score of 1 means a wild guess, which is the lowest level of confidence.

quiz.q: If your high confidence answers are often wrong, what should you do?
quiz.why: Overconfidence means you should be more cautious, so raising the threshold flags more doubtful answers.

lessons.t: Knowing when to guess and move on
lessons.intro: You will learn when a guess is the right call and how to make it quickly. A considered guess beats a long stall that costs easier marks.

cards.b: Cross out any option you know is wrong before choosing from the rest. Even removing one option raises your chance of a correct guess.
Guess when more thinking will not change the result within your time budget. Stop when the cost of time outweighs the gain from more thought.
Choose the same letter or the most plausible option each time you guess. A consistent rule removes the urge to deliberate.

fig.title: When to guess and move on
fig.note: Guess only after eliminating what you can.

ex.q: A question has four options and you can rule out two. If you guess randomly between the remaining two, what is your chance of being right?
ex.why: Two options remain, so a random guess is correct half the time, or 50 percent.

lessons.tip: A quick guess after elimination beats a slow guess with no elimination.

quiz.q: Roughly what is the chance of a random guess on a four option question?
quiz.why: With four options, each is equally likely, so one in four is 25 percent.

quiz.q: When should you stop thinking and guess?
o: When more thought will not change the result in time
quiz.why: Extra thought with no chance of improving the answer only costs time you need for later items.

lessons.t: Eliminating wrong options at speed
lessons.intro: You will learn quick tests that rule out options in seconds. Elimination lets you commit faster and with more confidence.

cards.b: Check whether each option is far too large or too small before fine detail. Obviously wrong options can be dropped in a single glance.
Match the units and sign of your working against each option. A mismatch in units or sign removes that option immediately.
Replace a variable with an easy number such as 1 or 10 to test each choice. This quick substitution exposes wrong options fast.

fig.title: Elimination checks
fig.note: Drop any option that fails a single test.

ex.q: Your working says the answer must be positive and under 100. Which option survives?
ex.why: -5 fails the positive test, and 120 and 200 fail the under-100 test, so 85 is the only survivor.

lessons.tip: Look for the cheapest test that removes the most options.

quiz.q: What does substituting a simple value like 10 test?
o: Whether each option works in the working
quiz.why: Plugging in a simple number checks each option against the working in seconds.

quiz.q: Which check is quickest to rule out an option?
o: A full calculation of each one
quiz.why: Signs and units can be checked at a glance, so they remove options before any heavy calculation.

lessons.t: Choosing fast between two close options
lessons.intro: You will learn a quick method for choosing between two options that look equally plausible. A simple tie-break keeps the decision short and fair.

cards.b: Ask which single feature separates the two options. Once you name it, the choice often becomes obvious within seconds.
If the feature does not decide it, pick the option that matches the question's wording most closely. Having a default prevents long debates.
When two options are equally supported, a quick choice costs little. Spending more time on a true tie rarely gains marks.

fig.title: Two close options
fig.note: The wording decides the tie.

ex.q: Which number is a multiple of both 3 and 5 and less than 30?
ex.why: Multiples of both 3 and 5 are multiples of 15, and the only one under 30 in this list is 15.

lessons.tip: Name the one feature that separates two options, then decide.

quiz.q: What is a decisive feature?
o: The font used in the question
The one feature that separates two options
quiz.why: A decisive feature is the single difference that settles the choice between two close options.

quiz.q: Why avoid long debates over a true tie?
quiz.why: When both options are equally supported, more thought seldom changes the outcome.

lessons.t: Trusting your first clear answer
lessons.intro: You will learn when your first answer deserves trust and when a second look is needed. Changing correct answers is a common and costly habit.

cards.b: A first answer built on a clear reading of the question is usually sound. Trust it when you can state the reason in one sentence.
Switch answers only when you spot a specific error in your working or reading. A vague feeling of doubt is not a reason to change.
Note how often a changed answer turns out right in your practice. Your record shows whether your second guesses help or hurt.

fig.title: Answer change check
fig.note: Change only when you can name the mistake.

ex.q: In practice you changed 10 answers. Only 2 of the changed answers were correct, and 8 were wrong. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: Changes are neither helpful nor harmful
Most of your changes hurt your score
ex.why: Only 2 of your 10 changes were right, so most changes cost marks when made without a specific reason.

lessons.tip: Change an answer only when you can name the mistake.

quiz.q: When is it good to change an answer?
o: When you feel a vague doubt
When you spot a specific error
When the test is almost over
quiz.why: A specific error is a real reason, while vague doubt is not new evidence.

quiz.q: Which habit helps you judge your second guesses?
o: Keeping a record of changed answers
quiz.why: A record shows whether your changes help or hurt, so you can adjust your habit.

lessons.t: Rehearsing a decision rule before the test
lessons.intro: You will learn to rehearse a simple decision rule until it runs automatically. A rule you have practised is much quicker to apply under time pressure.

cards.b: A good rule has three short steps, such as read, eliminate, choose. Keeping it brief means you can recall it under pressure.
Use the rule on every practice question and note where you hesitate. Hesitation points show exactly which step needs more work.
Repeat the same steps until you move through them without pausing. Automatic steps free attention for the content of the question.

fig.title: A three step decision rule
fig.note: Run it on every question, every time.

ex.q: Your rule is read, eliminate, choose. You have read the stem and eliminated two options. What is the next step?
ex.why: Your rule is read, eliminate, choose, so after reading and eliminating the next step is to choose from what remains.

lessons.tip: Practise the rule until you can recite it without thinking.

quiz.q: What is the main virtue of a short decision rule?
o: It is easy to recall under pressure
It removes the need for reading
quiz.why: A short rule can be recalled quickly, which matters when time is tight.

quiz.q: Where does hesitation during rehearsal show you?
o: The step that needs more work
quiz.why: Each hesitation points to a step that is not yet automatic.

lessons.t: Cutting hesitation with simple rules
lessons.intro: You will learn how clear if then rules speed up routine decisions. Each rule removes a pause, so your attention stays on the hard parts.

cards.b: Write rules like: if two options remain and one fits the wording, choose it. Such rules turn a vague pause into a clear action.
Limit yourself to three or four rules that cover most cases. Too many rules become a burden and slow you down.
Once a rule fires, act on it without reconsidering the whole question. Reopening settled decisions is the main source of hesitation.

fig.title: From doubt to action
fig.note: A rule turns a pause into one action.

ex.q: Your rule says: if one option matches the wording exactly and the others do not, choose it. A matches the wording, B and C do not, and D is unclear. What should you do?
o: Flag A and reread the stem
ex.why: Only A matches the wording, so the rule says to choose it without reopening the other options.

lessons.tip: Write the rule once, then trust it on every item.

quiz.q: What does a well written rule turn a pause into?
quiz.why: An if then rule converts hesitation into one specific action.

quiz.q: Why keep your rule set small?
o: Large sets are easier to forget
Few rules are easy to remember and apply
quiz.why: A few clear rules are fast to recall, while many rules slow you down.

lessons.t: Timing decisions through a sequence
lessons.intro: You will learn how to keep decisions on pace across a run of similar items. Steady timing stops one slow choice from pulling the rest off track.

cards.b: Give each item a decision budget, such as thirty seconds, and check it against the clock. A fixed budget makes it obvious when you have overrun.
Every five items, compare time spent with the budget you planned. Small corrections early avoid large corrections later.
Repeated items come faster once a pattern forms, so bank that gained time. Use the saved seconds on the next hard item.

fig.title: Planned minutes by checkpoint
fig.note: Each five items should cost 2.5 minutes at 30 seconds each.

ex.q: You have 30 seconds per item and 15 items. After 10 items, how many minutes should you have used at the planned pace?
ex.why: Ten items at 30 seconds each is 300 seconds, which is 5 minutes at the planned pace.

lessons.tip: Check the clock at fixed points rather than after every item.

quiz.q: How many minutes is 15 items at 30 seconds each?
quiz.why: 15 times 30 seconds is 450 seconds, which is 7.5 minutes.

quiz.q: What does banking saved time let you do?
o: Spend more on a hard item later
quiz.why: Saved seconds give a buffer, so a hard item later can take more time without blowing your plan.

lessons.t: Recovering quickly after a wrong call
lessons.intro: You will learn how to move on after a wrong decision without letting it damage the next items. Quick recovery protects both your score and your focus.

cards.b: Errors happen even to careful test takers, so treat each one as information rather than a verdict. Dwelling on it steals time from the next item.
Take one slow breath and look at the next question with fresh attention. A short reset stops a bad answer spilling into the next few items.
Note the mistake briefly and review it during spare time at the end. Reviewing later turns the error into a lesson rather than a worry.

fig.title: Recovering from a wrong call
fig.note: Move on within seconds, not minutes.

ex.q: A test has 20 questions in 30 minutes. You lost 4 minutes worrying about one mistake. How many minutes are left for the remaining items?
ex.why: The test has 30 minutes and 4 were lost to the mistake, leaving 30 minus 4, which is 26 minutes.

lessons.tip: A wrong answer costs one item, but dwelling on it can cost several.

quiz.q: What does a short reset help prevent?
o: A bad answer spilling into the next items
quiz.why: A breath and a fresh look stop one error from hurting the items that follow.

quiz.q: When is the best time to review a mistake?
o: During spare time at the end
quiz.why: Reviewing later in spare time turns the error into learning without costing current items.

lessons.t: Putting decision speed together in a test
lessons.intro: You will learn to combine pacing, scanning and quick decisions into one test routine. This final lesson shows how the skills work together under real time limits.

cards.b: Decide your pace per item, your flag rule and your review time before the test begins. A written plan means you rarely have to decide under pressure.
Use your scanning method to find the relevant information, then apply your decision rule. Each stage hands clean information to the next.
After each test or practice set, compare your pace, flags and changes with your plan. Small adjustments each time build a faster and more accurate routine.

fig.title: Your test routine grid
fig.note: Each stage feeds the next within one question.

ex.q: A test has 50 questions in 25 minutes. What is your base budget per question, and how many minutes should be used after 20 questions?
ex.why: 25 minutes divided by 50 questions is 0.5 minutes each, so 20 questions use 20 times 0.5, which is 10 minutes.

lessons.tip: A routine you have rehearsed is the one you will trust under pressure.

quiz.q: Which should you plan before the test starts?
o: Your pace, flag rule and review time
The exact answers to every question
quiz.why: A plan made in advance means you rarely decide under pressure.

quiz.q: What do you review after a practice set?
o: Pace, flags and changes against your plan
quiz.why: Comparing pace, flags and changes with your plan shows which parts of the routine to adjust.
